chunks: From him, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

"When a debt is claimed against you and the claimant has nothing to prove it with, and he wants to make you swear an oath, then if the amount reaches thirty dirhams, give it to him and do not swear; and if it is more than that, swear and do not give it."

key_terms.أُدُّيَ: was claimed / was presented as a debt
key_terms.يُحَلِّفَكَ: to make you swear an oath

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic legal ruling on paying a debt when the claimant has no proof and wants the debtor to swear an oath?
ai.summary: This ruling from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) in *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* establishes a pragmatic legal threshold of thirty dirhams to balance judicial efficiency with the preservation of the debtor's honor. By exempting small claims from the solemnity of an oath, the tradition minimizes litigation costs and social friction, while requiring an oath for larger sums ensures serious verification of significant debts. This reflects the Shia juristic principle of *sulh* (amicable settlement) and avoiding unnecessary *yamin* (oaths) in minor disputes.
